places.now: fictional; the City of London near Cornhill and the Royal Exchange
places.reason: Dombey and Son is invented, and Dickens places the firm in the City near the Royal Exchange without giving an address.

places.now: fictional; the City of London near Cornhill and the Royal Exchange
places.reason: 'Dombey's House' means the firm itself, which is fictional and set in the City, so this is the same approximate spot as its offices.

places.now: fictional; the seafront at Brighton/Hove, where large Regency terraces now stand
places.reason: The school is invented, and Dickens describes a tall seafront house in Brighton, so this is a guess at the Brunswick/King's Road area.

places.now: the Middle East, mainly Egypt (Cairo)
places.reason: The phrase is a vague region and the Jakarta match is wrong, so no single point fits.

places.now: the East End: Whitechapel, Stepney, Wapping and surrounding districts
places.reason: The East End had no fixed boundary, and the riverside districts around Whitechapel and Wapping are roughly its centre; the Finchley match is wrong.

places.now: no longer exists; Old Palace Yard beside the Palace of Westminster
places.reason: The coffee house is probably invented, but Palace Yard is a real place beside Westminster Hall.

places.now: filled in; the Jacob's Island area of Bermondsey near Mill Street and St Saviour's Dock
places.reason: The tidal ditch surrounded Jacob's Island in Bermondsey and was filled in during the later 19th century, so the exact line is uncertain.

places.now: demolished in the 1920s; site is Coram's Fields, with the Foundling Museum beside it
places.reason: The Foundling Hospital stood on Guilford Street in Bloomsbury and is well documented.

places.now: demolished 1912; site is near Postman's Park and the BT Centre on St Martin's Le Grand
places.reason: Smirke's GPO building of 1829 stood on the east side of St Martin's Le Grand.

places.now: demolished; site is on the Strand by Trafalgar Square and Charing Cross station
places.reason: The Golden Cross was a famous coaching inn at Charing Cross, and its successor on the Strand was demolished in the 1930s.

places.now: no longer exists; Holborn near the Gray's Inn gateway
places.reason: There was a Gray's Inn Coffee House near Gray's Inn in Holborn, but I do not know its exact spot.

places.now: uncertain; possibly Hampstead Grove, or the Grove in Highgate
places.reason: The name is common across London and Dickens gives no further detail, so this is an educated guess at Hampstead.

places.now: Hampton, in the London Borough of Richmond upon Thames
places.reason: Oliver and Sikes pass through Hampton on the Thames on the way to Shepperton, which is a real place.

places.now: Ercolano; the Herculaneum archaeological park near Naples
places.reason: This is the well-known Roman town buried by Vesuvius, and the gazetteer match is correct.

places.now: South Square, Gray's Inn
places.reason: Holborn Court was the old name of the court now called South Square in Gray's Inn, though I am less sure of its exact position within the Inn.

places.now: Harper Road, Southwark; Newington Gardens occupies the old gaol site
places.reason: Horsemonger Lane ran past the Surrey county gaol in Newington and was later renamed Harper Road.

places.now: no longer exist; the Thames estuary off the Kent marshes
places.reason: Convict hulks lay at Woolwich, Chatham and elsewhere, and Dickens sets his hulks in the lower Thames/Medway off the Cooling marshes without a precise location.

places.now: demolished 1862; site is Charing Cross railway station
places.reason: Hungerford Market stood on the Strand riverfront and was cleared for Charing Cross station.

places.now: the Inns of Court: Lincoln's Inn, Gray's Inn, the Temple, with Chancery Lane at their centre
places.reason: This is a collective term for four legal societies in Holborn and the Temple, so any single point is only approximate.

places.now: the counties of Kent and Surrey
places.reason: This names two counties, not one point, and the helipad match is wrong.

places.now: Lake Geneva (Lac Léman), on the Swiss-French border
places.reason: Dickens began Dombey and Son at Lausanne on the lake in 1846.

places.now: the Old Hall, Lincoln's Inn, still standing
places.reason: In Dickens's time the Lord Chancellor sat in Lincoln's Inn Old Hall, which survives.

places.now: no longer a hotel; shops and offices on New Bond Street near Clifford Street
places.reason: Long's Hotel was a well-known fashionable hotel at the corner of Bond Street and Clifford Street, though I am not sure of the exact plot.

places.now: the Cooling Marshes on the Hoo Peninsula, Kent, near Cooling village and the Thames estuary
places.reason: The Great Expectations marsh country is generally identified with the marshes around Cooling and Higham in north Kent, though it is partly imagined.

places.now: fictional; the Thames-side area of Twickenham
places.reason: The cottage is invented and Dickens places it near Twickenham without giving a location, so this is a guess at the town centre.
